It's now time to enter the constraints of the problem.
We'll give you some guidance for the first constraint.  Then you can do the remaining constraints on your own.
The manufacturing capacity is 250.  This should be put in cell G22.  But don't write "250" in cell G22.  Instead, write "= I11."

In general, don't write values for the right hand sides of constraints.  Instead, reference the original data.  That way, if the original data is changed, the values in the constraints are automatically changed.
Now express the total manufacturing capacity in terms of the decision variables, and put it in cell E22.   You could write  "= .1 * E19 + .2 * F19 + .7 * G19".  This would be correct.
It is much better to write " = E11 * E19 + F11 * F19 + G11 * G19".  In this way, if the original data is changed, then the manufacturing capacity is updated at once.
A very useful shortcut is the SUMPRODUCT formula.  In Cell E22, you can put the formula "= SUMPRODUCT(E11:G11, E19:G19)"
Try using SUMPRODUCT.  If you did it correctly, you should have a 2.6 in the cell.  Try changing the values of the decision variables and notice that the manufacturing capacity will change.
Finally, put "<=" in Cell F22.  The purpose of this is to make the spreadsheet easier to read.  It has no impact on any of the computations.
In general, it is a good idea to use "<=", ">=" and "=" when expressing constraints on the spreadsheet, for ease of reading.
Now, select Solver again.  To the right of "Subject to the constraints" click on "Add."  The cell reference is where the formula for the constraint is held.  In this case, it is in E22.
The type of constraint is "<=".  The "Constraint" refers to the cell holding the RHS of the constraint.  In this case, it is cell G22.  After entering "G22", click on "OK".
We have now added the first constraint to the problem.  We could have added it in many different ways.  For example, you could have listed I11 as the "constraint".

If you look inside of cell E23, you will notice that the second set of ranges in the SUMPRODUCT refer to row 20.  But you wanted it to be row 19.
You can fix this by using a "$" before each"19" in the formula in cell E22, and then copy down the constraint.
Now put in the correct formulas in cells E23:E27 and put in the correct right hand sides in cells G23 to G27.  Verify that the formulas are correct by modifying the decision variables.
Have one of the variables be "1" and the rest of the variables be "0".  This often reveals whether the constraints are correct.
Open Solver and add the five new constraints corresponding to rows 23 to 27.
Now it is time to enter the revenue function.  Enter the formula for the revenue function (using SUMPRODUCT) into cell I15.  Verify it is correct by modifying decision variables.
Then open up Solver again, and put "I15" into "Set Target Cell."
We are almost ready to click on "Solve."  But first, you need to click on "Max" which is to the right of "Equal To."  (If it was already selected, you don't need to do anything).
If you had clicked on "Min", Solver would have determined the solution with the minimum revenue.
You still need to say that all variables are nonnegative and  that the problem is a linear program.  This can occur either on the dialogue box in front of you or by clicking on options.

Different versions of Excel have different ways of doing this.  In Excel 2010 and 2011 this is done on the first dialogue box.  To say that it is an LP, write that Simplex should be used as the solution method.
It really is important to click on "assume linear model."  For now, please take my word for it.
Cathy knows what she is talking about.
